title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaving US for Spain, bringing deportation battle to an end
description: Kilmar Ábrego García, who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in 2025, is leaving the US for Spain, ending a long-running deportation battle with t
body: Kilmar Ábrego García, who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in 2025, is leaving the US for Spain, ending a long-running deportation battle with the Trump administration.He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.His deportation and return became a flash point in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release. "A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."The BBC has reached out to Ábrego García's lawyers and the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return. The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons. For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country. At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

schema.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García leaving US for Spain, bringing deportation battle to an end

title: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 2 hours agoDomestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of house
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 2 hours agoDomestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of households, with regulator Ofgem to announce the precise increase shortly.A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, in a forecast made ahead of the official announcement.Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, will come into force at the coldest time of year. Customers pay for what they use and charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.The government will make a £100 payment to millions of households to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.The warm home discount will also take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended."We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice. "Every day our advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises. Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left."About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap. Those on fixed tariffs will be unaffected, but the impact may be felt when that tariff expires and the replacement is more expensive.If forecasts prove correct, then a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity and paying by direct debit will see a bill rise of about £37 a month from January to the end of March. If sustained for a year, it would mean the typical annual bill will rise by £443 to £2,166 compared with the current cap.However, individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost is likely to be about £126. Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver of the forecast higher prices. The war in Iran has led to higher international gas prices. With storage levels relatively low ahead of the winter, suppliers had to buy ahead at steeply higher prices.The average price of gas is 166% higher than late last year, before the Iran war began, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.Andrew Sissons, from research foundation Nesta, said that the expected change in bills for households could have a wider impact."Higher energy bills will reduce household spending on everything else, which will have a knock-on effect across the rest of the economy," he said.On Sunday, Chris O'Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, told the BBC he was "hugely concerned" about the impact of the January rise in prices.There was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, he said, with some unable to pay, and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".Energy UK calculations suggest that £67 of the average annual energy bill covers the cost of this debt. Those who pay their bill every three months, rather than by monthly direct debit, face the biggest addition.Total energy debt was likely to rise towards £7bn by the end of the year, the trade body said.Support in placePredictions suggest domestic energy prices could stay high throughout next year. Even if wholesale gas prices were to fall, then network costs for running and upgrading the electricity system are expected to be high.The government has temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.The £100 support payment will be made, automatically, to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.But Citizens Advice said that those on prepayment meters in particular, who often top up the most during the coldest months, would see the money disappear quickly.It said it was bracing for a wave of more people seeking emergency help this winter, because they could not top up their meters

schema.headline: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced

title: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
description: Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local
body: Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process."The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said."Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

schema.headline: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds

title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
description: Figure caption, Watch: 'The truth will have its own power,' Burnham saysByVictoria DerbyshireCarys NallyBBC Newsnight and Sean SeddonAndy Burnham has
body: Figure caption, Watch: 'The truth will have its own power,' Burnham saysByVictoria DerbyshireCarys NallyBBC Newsnight and Sean SeddonAndy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into. "I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."BBC Newsnight special on nuclear test veteransVictoria Derbyshire speaks to veterans as an independent panel is announced into health impactsWatch now on iPlayerVeterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the LABRATS group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers. He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years. "Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."Figure caption, Watch: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about search for justiceBarbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of. "Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."Image caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told campaigners in Downing Street that he would launch an independent investigationThe MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.The MoD released some official documents in July 2026, though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.'Serious allegations against the state'The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit. He said the panel would "help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed".Asked if the government would pay compensation should the panel recommend it, Streeting said he would not pre-judge its report but that he felt "absolutely sure the findings will be uncomfortable" and the government "will have to take that on the chin".

schema.headline: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel

title: Inflation: How rising food prices are squeezing Indian households
description: India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.The latest government data, external shows retail inflatio
body: India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists. With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences. In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation. That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment."Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food. The numbers bear this out. According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%. In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal. Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says. When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economyOnions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings. The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives. Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer. "The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later. Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to SharmaThere are other pressures. Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample. There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta. "Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting. Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes. Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

schema.headline: Inflation: How rising food prices are squeezing Indian households

title: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga IvshinaBBC Russian and Yaroslava Kiryukh
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga IvshinaBBC Russian and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC RussianAt least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.How we came to a figure near half a millionThe Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesIn most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

schema.headline: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine

title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
description: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable
body: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life."I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming."When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here."We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be." These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem."You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product."The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then."It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier."We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them."We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence."Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

schema.headline: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe

title: Trump's Nvidia intervention ties his political fortunes to the AI boom
description: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, Preside
body: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap."I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet? Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter."Every time you have a Chinese woman that's goodlooking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology. State governments could also launch their own investigations.Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself."I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X."Congress has much to investigate," he said.While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed. Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large. In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption."Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year. The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules."It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday. "Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy. He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic). And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters. He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%. Last Friday alone, it fell 14%. US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed. And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

schema.headline: Trump's Nvidia intervention ties his political fortunes to the AI boom

title: US preparing to unveil new tariffs on global trading partners
description: The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading
body: The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan among the 16 jurisdictions affected.The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute.Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.In the run up to the Shenzhen summit the US accused China of not fully living up the terms of what it agreed in South Korea in October 2025.Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

schema.headline: US preparing to unveil new tariffs on global trading partners

title: Man City 2-2 Napoli: Enzo Maresca's side grinding to a halt
description: 'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a haltImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw
body: 'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a haltImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw for Manchester City against NapoliByManchester City reporter at Etihad StadiumManchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.City's recent defensive issues also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.Maresca said: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end."Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on."The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end."'Dull and predictable'City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few issues in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.Their injury issues mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is quickly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes."It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live."If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend."You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out."Is Haaland lacking service?Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net."I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy."Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy."City are sixth in the Champions League table, before Wednesday's games, but in the Premier League they have failed to win their past four.It does not get any easier this weekend, facing a daunting trip to leaders Arsenal on Sunday as they aim to find some form.Haaland added: "It's the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away."We need a top performance from every single player."

schema.headline: Man City 2-2 Napoli: Enzo Maresca's side grinding to a halt

title: Beau Lamarre: Sydney police officer convicted of murder of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies
description: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murderImage source, NSW Supreme CourtImage caption, Thous
body: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murderImage source, NSW Supreme CourtImage caption, Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau LamarreByHelen LivingstoneSydneyIt was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.Image source, Supplied: Jesse BairdImage caption, Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned downDuring a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found."What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.Dark infatuationBaird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off. But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November. He'd discovered the Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.'The beginning of the plan for murder'Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back. On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."Image source, Supplied: Jesse BairdImage caption, Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killedEarly on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.Covering tracksAfter that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess". Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out."I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.Image source, NSW Supreme CourtImage caption, Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murdersLamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.Lamarre faces life in prisonImage source, GettyImage caption, The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in SydneyBy this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline."I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia.""Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders. The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

schema.headline: Beau Lamarre: Sydney police officer convicted of murder of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies

title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
description: ByDaniel Thomas and Anuk WeerawardanaBusiness reportersDomestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pu
body: ByDaniel Thomas and Anuk WeerawardanaBusiness reportersDomestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.'We power down at peak times'Image source, Kelly Anne HarveyImage caption, Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heatingLike many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000. She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again. To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill. The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often. They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend. "On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothingStacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027. The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year. Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit. She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water."I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."'I order heating oil in bulk'Image source, SuppliedAround 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets."When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire. "At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries. Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders. Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive. Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.   Get in touchWhat are you doing to cope with rising energy bills?

schema.headline: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down

title: Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games
description: It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.In th
body: It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal. The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years. But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game. Against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes. In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target. Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance"."The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition that we played today and what we've done out there, is just something to be very, very pleased [about] because there is very little more that you can demand from the team," Arteta said. "But obviously, the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance in the amount of chances (and) situations."There is an element of luck; there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist because I think what the team has done and shown today, I think it's the right direction." Arteta made six changes to the side that drew with Newcastle, with one of the biggest calls to rest striker Kai Havertz and bring in Viktor Gyokeres. The striker has had a difficult season so far, with four of his seven starts coming in the Champions League against opposition where Arsenal have been favourites. However, Gyokeres scored a powerful effort from outside the area to give Arsenal the lead against Dortmund. Overall though, it ended up being a mixed night for the 28-year-old as he missed a header from inside the six-yard-box that would have surely won the game for the Gunners late on. Arteta was asked if the chances his side are missing were down to mentality, misfortune or composure. "Mentality, I don't know," he said."There is an element of luck here because how some of the goals they haven't gone inside, I don't know."The execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think it was really, really good." Arteta was also full of praise for Gyokeres, with particular emphasis on the striker's link-up play; an element of his game at times criticised."What I love the most is how connected he was to the team," Arteta said. "We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch. "There was a lot to like in that performance and that's the Viktor that we needed." Noni Madueke has been Arsenal's best attacker in recent weeks. The winger, who was left out of the last England squad, is enjoying a run in the Arsenal starting XI with Bukayo Saka out injured and is taking his opportunity.Madueke has registered a goal and two assists in his past three games and was again the best Arsenal forward against Dortmund. The Gunners host Manchester City on Sunday and are currently six points clear at the top of the Premier League table. Madueke, who was frustrated with the performance against Dortmund, said the clash with third-placed City is a great chance to get back to winning ways and shake off any frustration."I think these are the best games. I'm really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same," Madueke told Amazon Prime. "We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We're champions, we're at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates. "There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction."

schema.headline: Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games

title: Great British Bake Off winner crowned after high-stakes final
description: Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off finalMoyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of
body: Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off finalMoyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies.Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode."I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said."I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends."He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".The high-stakes final saw the three contestants tasked with making a citrus celebration cake, creme brulee donuts and a "spectacular tribute to iconic British landscapes".Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward."I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support."Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said."Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."He shared his gratitude at being able to learn from Lawson and Hollywood."I will never forget my time there and the friendships made which will always continue," the winner added.Prior to the final, Odeniran told BBC Essex he planned to view it at a huge "watch party" at his local church.Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

title: Substance at Don Toliver Manchester show may be linked to robberies, police say
description: Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public."We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two E
body: Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public."We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.In a statement on Tuesday evening, Co-op Live said it was conducting a "full review" into the incident."The safety and security of our guests, artists and staff remain our highest priority, and we take that responsibility extremely seriously."The venue, which opened in 2024, apologised to fans for what should have been an "enjoyable evening" and said it expects no disruption to future events.The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.Many were advised to seal their clothes in a bag overnight.Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage."We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas."Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."Posting on Instagram on Monday, Toliver said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night at Co-op Live."The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."He also asked that people stop bringing substances into his shows.GMP urged anyone who feels unwell or develops symptoms following the concert to seek medical advice.

schema.headline: Substance at Don Toliver Manchester show may be linked to robberies, police say
